sources.headline: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
sources.text: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, including a request for election officials to separate ballots that rank retired teacher Dan J Sullivan.Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress."I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."Alaska's Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an official inquiry earlier this week into the alleged scheme. Heyman did not immediately provide details of specific crimes his office would investigate.Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to her campaign.But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola. The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the recruitment effort, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner. No charges had been filed as of Friday evening. "There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that are ongoing," Michael Heyman, the US attorney for the district of Alaska, said at a Friday afternoon press conference. Later that day, lawyers for the Trump administration asked a federal judge to issue an order before Monday that would direct state election officials "to preserve and segregate" all ballots that rank Dan J Sullivan.Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued in court documents that the move would be to investigate whether such ranking "was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary"."These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration," he said. Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests. "I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.The spectre of a federal crimes could come into play if there was potential evidence of campaign finance violations, Kendall, as well as other legal experts, told the BBC. But such evidence has not yet emerged.Kendall believed the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm". The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate. The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up. As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.

sources.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories It is the final stretch before Election Day on Tuesday and candidates are making final campaign stops and delivering closing arguments. President Trump has been campaigning for at-risk Republicans, but he has abruptly switched to virtual rallies.

🎧 Trump's tour to boost voter turnout has focused largely on competitive Republican-leaning states, NPR's Saige Miller tells Up First. He's hosting 19 telerallies alongside in-person events. The shift in strategy, plus polling data, suggests that Republicans may face challenges, at least in the House, Miller says. Trump knows he's a key motivator for his party, but his strategy could also backfire by energizing Democrats.🎧 Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation following a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race. The article revealed that Democratic campaign operatives were attempting to recruit a candidate, whom Republicans claim could confuse voters and siphon support from GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan. The candidate also shares the name Dan Sullivan. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, aims to flip the seat. Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin spoke with election law experts, who found no applicable laws but noted that the conduct described crosses moral and ethical lines.➡️ The Department of Justice subpoenaed election workers in Los Angeles amid rising tensions with California officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on voter rolls.➡️ At the start of this election cycle, Democrats appeared unlikely to gain Senate seats because many races were in red states. Discover resources in your community here.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who oversaw planning at the Pentagon. Sylvia was also part of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. His removal comes as the U.S. and Israel prepare for a new potential round of attacks against Iran. Although Sylvia held a senior position in strategy, planning and policy, he was not directly involved in day-to-day operations regarding the Iran conflict. 🎧 The Pentagon is investigating a leak but has not provided details, NPR's Greg Myre says. Hegseth has dismissed several generals and admirals, often without explanation. These firings have disrupted senior military operations, Myre says. The U.S. currently has two aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea, with a third, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, en route. According to Myre, it is unusual for the U.S. to have multiple carriers in one region. The last time it stationed three in the Middle East was during the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have faced higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, after the Trump administration shut down a key part of the VA's home loan program. Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.
Behind the story by Rob Stein, NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor
Mary Long/Getty Images
I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs. But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story. I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.
I explored what these rule changes will mean for organ donors. You can read about it here. Weekend picks

sources.headline: Is it legal to recruit spoiler candidates in US elections?
sources.text: WASHINGTON - The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democrats recruited potential spoiler candidates to run in Alaska’s US Senate race, and has asked a US judge to prevent certification of the vote if incumbent Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses narrowly.The race, in which Democratic former US representative Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan, could prove critical for determining the balance of power in the Senate in the Nov 3 midterm elections.President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are battling to maintain majorities in both chambers.Here is an explanation of the legal issues at play and why the Justice Department will face challenges in its civil lawsuit or any criminal case.What is the state of the Alaska race?Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Daniel Sullivan, and another long-shot candidate.Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Peltola’s aides worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit the retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.Reuters has not verified the report.Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and Alaska’s Republican governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a state law enforcement investigation.Neither Trump nor Dunleavy specified which laws they believed may have been violated.A Justice Department official said no charging decision had been made.The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and said Republicans had also propped up other candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.Daniel J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.Peltola’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.Its lawyers have asked US District Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks the legal authority to bring the case.Alaska’s ballot will indicate that Daniel S. Sullivan is the incumbent.Could the Times report affect the outcome of the DOJ lawsuit?The Justice Department case seeking to prevent certification of election results if the incumbent Daniel S. Sullivan loses by a slim margin is pending.The department plans to seek a preliminary injunction, Michael Heyman, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska, told reporters on Oct 30.Alaska’s elections regulator earlier in 2026 blocked Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot, finding that his candidacy was not filed in good faith and was instead an attempt to “confuse or mislead.”State courts later restored him to the ballot, ruling that there was not enough evidence that he was trying to confuse voters and that there was no requirement under Alaska law that a candidacy be in good faith.Legal experts have said the Justice Department’s case is weak because the US Constitution clearly assigns the responsibility for administering elections to the states, not the federal government.Joshua Douglas, a law professor at the University of Kentucky, said the reporting asserting that Democrats helped recruit spoiler candidates was unlikely to help the Justice Department’s case.“Regardless of who encouraged him to run, the second Dan Sullivan validly qualified for the ballot. And this is a matter of state law,” Douglas said.Gleason’s decision on Peltola’s motion to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit could come as soon as Oct 31, though it is not certain when she will rule.What criminal laws could be at play?Legal experts said the Justice Department could seek to bring a criminal case under a federal statute that makes it illegal for any two people to conspire to deprive anyone of their constitutional rights, including the right to vote.The law, originally passed in 1871 to combat the Ku Klux Klan, makes it illegal to conspire to “injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any person” to prevent them from exercising a right.In addition, if anyone lied under oath in earlier state-level litigation over whether Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, they could be prosecuted for perjury, UCLA law professor Rick Hasen wrote in an Oct 8 blog post.A Justice Department official said the conduct under investigation could implicate statutes prohibiting fraud, dishonesty, and deprivations of civil rights.Would any prosecution be viable?Hasen said any federal criminal prosecution under the conspiracy-against-rights statute would likely fail because the free speech guarantees in the First Amendment to the US Constitution would likely protect the right to run for office with “impure motives.”Michael Fragoso, a former lawyer for Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, said “dirty tricks” – such as one major party trying to help a fringe candidate win over voters from the other major party – were generally legal.But he said convincing voters they were voting for their preferred candidate when they were not was different.“It’s suppressing disfavoured votes by tricking voters into thinking that they’re voting one way when in fact, they aren’t,” Fragoso, now a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Ethics and Public Policy Centre, wrote in an Oct 28 blog post in the National Review.Is there any legal precedent?In a case brought by the Justice Department under Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration, a social media influencer was convicted in 2023 in Brooklyn federal court of conspiring against civil rights by using social media posts to spread false information about the 2016 election to help Trump win.The Manhattan-based 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025 overturned that conviction, finding a lack of evidence he conspired with anyone.The appeals court’s decision did not address the influencer’s argument that the First Amendment would protect speech deceiving voters. REUTERS
